prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated without a lattice light shift

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration unchanged: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Round 1 did not change the scientific case, it sharpened the citation. The invention is that a lattice at the magic wavelength removes the differential light shift of the clock transition, so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms is held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated simultaneously. That is a different physical idea from a frequency comb, which is a readout tool the clock uses, and from single-ion control, which is a different regime with a single quantum system. The many-atom character is also what lets statistical uncertainty fall quickly, while the systematic effects that matter (collisions, spin-exchange, collective shifts) are many-body effects that had to be understood and controlled to reach about 1e-18. Independent laboratories have reproduced and surpassed this, so maturity and interpretation are not in question. The credit divides naturally into concept and first realisation (Katori) and performance and control (Ye), and no member proposes a different pair or a third name. The chair's question on the SI redefinition: I treat it as a consequence of the physics being settled and not as a reason either to award or to wait, and I would keep it out of the citation, as Danielsson suggests. The citation should say lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength mechanism, and not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general, so that ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups are not misrepresented.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged but narrower. First, the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes sit on either side of this one, and Olsson reads the clock as a refinement of an existing timekeeping capability; I answer that confinement without a trapping shift is a new idea and not a tuning of an old one, but this is a judgement and not a fact. Second, the credit is not complete: Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and others made the lattice clock a mature instrument, and no two-name list represents them. I regard this as the ordinary long tail of a prize, not a defect, and a third name is not supported by evidence in the files. Third, the priority sequence between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstrations is still recalled from general knowledge by me and by several colleagues, and nothing in the shortlist lets me verify it. If a documented check showed that the concept and first demonstration belong to others than Katori and Ye, I would withdraw the configuration. The pending redefinition of the second is a timing argument, not a scientific one, and I find it weak.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B007 because it opened a materials class and conceptual framework, whereas she reads the lattice clock as a refinement of capability that Hall, Haensch and Wineland already advanced; she would still rather award a visible credit question than a prettier configuration for a more incremental step.
responses.response: I agree with her that B007 is scientifically first-rank, and I accept her point that the 2016 prize is not a real bar, since the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-symmetric helical edge are a distinct step. Where I disagree is the premise that attribution is only a prettiness issue. Her own uncertainty list asks whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal was indispensable to the Molenkamp observation; if it was, she says herself that three names cannot be fair, and Zhang's death means the committee cannot repair it. A prize that I know to be misattributed is a scientific judgement, not cosmetics. On incrementalism, the clock is not a better measurement of an old quantity: it rests on a new confinement idea that took neutral-atom clocks from the microwave standard to about 1e-18, and many-atom interrogation is what made that attainable. I keep B007 as my first alternative and would move it up only if the committee could settle the HgTe credit with a documented argument.

responses.point: Johansson proposes a two-part prize, the lattice clock (Katori, Ye) plus Hosono for iron-based superconductors, using exactly three names, and argues the open pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap, not a gap in the discovery.
responses.response: I agree with him on the first part and I accept that Hosono's attribution is unambiguous and the discovery well replicated; my earlier response treated maturity too lightly there, and I withdraw the comparison with B012. I still do not join the second part. Johansson concedes that the two parts have almost nothing in common and that Hosono has thin support, and I read the pairing as being driven by the three-name arithmetic and not by a shared scientific theme. The follow-on work that raised the transition temperature in iron-based compounds came from several groups, so a sole-laureate share is arguably unbalanced, as he himself notes. Adding a part whose own supporters call it weak would dilute a prize that is already complete. I would leave B037 for a year in which it has broader backing, and I do not put it among my alternatives.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B056 with a two-person credit and asks, with Kroll, that the early priority sequence be checked before the citation is fixed; she also notes that a broader credit to the clock community would require a third name the files do not support.
responses.response: We agree on the two names and on keeping them at two. On priority, I share her unease and the answer to the chair's question is that I cannot verify the sequence from the supplied material. I would not let this hold up a decision, because what makes the credit defensible is structural: Katori's proposal and first realisation concern the magic-wavelength lattice, Ye's work brought it to the accuracy and control that made it the reference instrument, and no member proposes any other pair. I would make the citation wording carry the load: 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' with the mechanism named. Her question about the redefinition of the second is one I answer as coincident evidence, not a cause: the physics was settled before the redefinition was scheduled.

responses.point: Kroll supports B056 and, like me, wants the citation to name the lattice clock and not optical clocks generally; he also flags his research stay in John Hall's laboratory as a possible recusal question.
responses.response: I agree with his wording and I do not see his stay in the Hall laboratory as a recusal trigger. Hall is part of the 2005 background that Olsson cites as overlap, but Kroll has no documented relationship with Katori or Ye, and the comb is exactly the readout tool I argue is distinct from the lattice idea. I would only ask that he help the committee state, in the discussion and not only in the citation, why the lattice clock is a step beyond the combs and ion control, since the chair's first question is aimed at those who doubt this and Kroll is well placed to answer it in a documented way.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B007 with a concept-centred citation and would accept the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap as a regrettable unfairness, because the invariant and the state are Kane and Mele's.
responses.response: I respect this reading and it is the best case for B007: if the citation is centred on the Z2 invariant and the time-reversal-symmetric helical state, the gap is smaller. But the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe was seen because a specific platform was proposed, and a prize that names the experiment and omits the proposers is more exposed than one centred on concept alone, while a concept-only citation would then leave Molenkamp's measurement uncredited. Either route leaves a gap, and the lattice clock does not. That is a tie-breaker between two mature and original achievements and not a quality ranking, and I would be comfortable if the committee settled the other way.

uncertainties: The priority sequence between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations is from general knowledge and not verified; I would reconsider if a documented check contradicts the Katori and Ye split.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I find the distinction real but it remains a judgement, and Olsson does not share it.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal was indispensable to the HgTe observation, which decides how high B007 can stand.
Whether the pending SI redefinition of the second will in practice lead other members to hold back a metrology prize this year; I do not think it should.
How strongly I should discount my own preference for a statistical, many-atom view of clock operation; it is a reason I find the invention elegant, not independent evidence of prize-worthiness.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict. None of Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hosono or the other credited names on the shortlist appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutional connections, and my research (turbulent aerosols, random matrices, stochastic dynamics, neural networks) is distant from the preferred candidate. I have taught and written on neural networks, which does not bear on any shortlisted entry. I see no recusal trigger among the disclosed flags that bears on my vote.
